results.claim: Let D(m,n) be the maximum push number of a sortable m×n instance, N=mn, s=min{m,n}, and t=max{m,n}. Then D(m,n)=O(N·min{s,log t}).
results.proof_sketch:
Assume 2≤m≤n. Transpose A and give a token with original target (r,c) target (c,r). Write p=n,q=m for the transposed board B. The FillColumns proof does not use p≤q: each column is pushed at most p−1 times. If f columns are underfull, each q buffer-row pushes lower the wrong-body potential Ψ by at least f/2. In a phase q/2^i≤f<q/2^{i−1}, Ψ<(p−1)q/2^{i−1}, so fewer than 4p complete q-push blocks occur. Summing O(log q) phases gives O(pq log q). FloatMinimums costs O(pq) and makes all B-columns body-full. The separate cleanup claim below then sorts B's heads in O(pq) without changing any body set. Every B-column therefore contains precisely its target-column tokens, so after transposing back every original row has precisely its target-row tokens. This membership stage costs O(N log m).

Now sort the m rows. An even required row permutation is the product of two involutions with equally many transpositions; opposite-direction SwapPairs calls apply them in O(N) and cancel every off-row shift. If the permutation is odd and n is even, one unit row push leaves an even residual. If n is odd and m is even, apply the equal-involution part and one transposition; the latter's auxiliary-body shift is an even permutation of m−1 cells, so two transposed, opposite-direction involution calls reverse it and restore every off-row cell in O(N). If m,n are odd, global parity implies an even number of odd rows. Sort each such row up to the same adjacent swap P_i. For adjacent rows, (a b c)(a d c)=(a b)(c d), with each L-cycle a four-push commutator; chaining these gadgets realizes P_rP_s in O(m). Pairing odd rows costs O(m²)≤O(N). Thus all rows cost O(mN), giving O(Nm). Combining this with the source's O(N log n) algorithm and symmetry proves the claim.

results.claim: For every fixed s≥2, boards with min{m,n}=s have asymptotically tight push number D(m,n)=Θ(mn).
results.proof_sketch: Claim 0 supplies D(m,n)=O(Ns)=O(N) for fixed s. For the reverse inequality, translate the sorted board by floor(n/2) columns and floor(m/2) rows. Claim 2 gives exact distance m·floor(n/2)+n·floor(m/2), which is Ω(mn) whenever min{m,n}=s≥2 is fixed. Hence D(m,n)=Θ(mn).

results.claim: Every instance A has the displacement certificate pn(A)≥ceil(H(A)/n)+ceil(V(A)/m). Moreover, a global translation by a columns and b rows has exact push number m·d_n(a)+n·d_m(b), where d_k(z)=min(z mod k,k−(z mod k)).
results.proof_sketch: Use pn(A)=∞ for an unsortable instance. Otherwise, a row push changes the total cyclic horizontal displacement H by at most n, and column pushes leave H unchanged. Thus any sorting word has at least ceil(H/n) row pushes. Symmetrically it has at least ceil(V/m) column pushes, and these counts add. For a global translation, H=mn·d_n(a) and V=mn·d_m(b), yielding the stated lower bound. Rotating every row and column back along shortest directions attains it. The half-translation therefore has exact distance m·floor(n/2)+n·floor(m/2).

results.claim: A sharper general counting lower bound is D(m,n)≥ceil(log_{d−1}(1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d)), where d=2(m+n), Q=(mn)! if m or n is even, and Q=(mn)!/2 otherwise.
results.proof_sketch: The parity characterization gives exactly Q sortable configurations. A geodesic word has no generator immediately followed by its inverse, so the number of possible endpoints of words of length at most L is at most 1+d·((d−1)^L−1)/(d−2). Duplicate transformations for size-two rows or columns only increase this overcount. Since every sortable configuration is within distance D, rearranging the resulting inequality gives the displayed bound. Stirling's estimate makes it (2−o(1))N for bounded aspect ratio.

results.claim: Global translations are not generally diametral: D(2,3)=7, whereas every translated 2×3 board has distance at most 5.
results.proof_sketch: Exact breadth-first search with the seven distinct 2×3 unit generators visits all 720 configurations with level sizes [1,7,31,115,274,253,36,3], so the diameter is 7. From the identity, R1-left, C1-up, R1-left, C1-up, C3-up, R1-right, C1-up reaches ((3,2,1),(6,5,4)), whose exact distance is 7. Exhausting the six global translations gives maximum distance 2·floor(3/2)+3·floor(2/2)=5.

results.claim: Given a p×q matrix in which every column is body-full, its buffer row can be sorted in O(pq) pushes while preserving the set of tokens in every column body.
results.proof_sketch: Body-fullness places all nonbuffer target-column tokens in the corresponding bodies, so the q heads are exactly the q buffer tokens. Let π be the permutation required to sort them. If π is even, write π=συ where σ and υ are involutions with the same number k of transpositions. Apply σ by SwapPairs with upward body shifts and υ with downward shifts. Each call uses the same auxiliary columns C1,…,Ck, so all body shifts cancel. If π is odd, write π=συτ with the same property and τ a transposition. The first two calls again cancel; one further SwapPairs call applies τ and cyclically shifts one body, preserving its token set. Every call costs O(kp+q), with k≤q/2, while the final transposition costs O(p+q). Thus the total is O(pq), the heads are sorted, and no body loses or gains a token.

final_writeup:
The audit correctly refutes the previous construction as written: transposed FloatMinimums makes columns body-full, not head-correct, so undoing the transpose immediately can leave tokens in the wrong original rows. The 2×3 witness exposes exactly that failure.

The repair is to clean the transposed buffer row before undoing the transpose. Once all transposed columns are body-full, their heads are precisely the buffer tokens. The new cleanup lemma sorts those heads using two opposite-direction SwapPairs calls for the equal-involution part of the head permutation and, when necessary, one additional call for a residual transposition. The first two calls cancel their body shifts; the last may cyclically shift one body but cannot change its token set. Consequently every transposed column contains its complete target-column set. On the audited state B=((2,1),(3,4),(5,6)), an exact unit-push realization produces ((1,2),(5,4),(3,6)); its column sets are {1,3,5} and {2,4,6}. Thus the witness is repaired rather than ignored.

The dimension-independent FillColumns potential analysis gives this membership stage cost O(N log s). After transposing back, each original row contains exactly its target-row tokens. Each even within-row permutation can be performed in O(N) pushes while restoring every other position. Odd permutations are handled by a unit row push when the row length is even, by the positional odd construction when the board height is even, and in odd-by-odd boards by pairing the necessarily even number of odd rows. The paired adjacent-transposition chains cost only O(s²) altogether. Sorting all s rows therefore costs O(Ns).

Combining the resulting O(Ns) construction with the source's O(N log t) algorithm yields

D(m,n)=O(N·min{s,log t}).

Together with the exact half-translation lower bound, this proves D(m,n)=Θ(mn) for every fixed smaller dimension s≥2. The displacement certificate, reduced-word counting bound, and exact 2×3 non-diametral-translation result are retained unchanged.

This is genuine partial target coverage, but it does not solve the requested general open problem. When s≥log t, the best bounds supplied here remain Ω(N) and O(N log t), so a logarithmic gap persists. Accordingly the claimed resolution is PARTIAL, not FULL.
